entries.title: 2 drivers killed, 3 minors hospitalized in 5-vehicle crash in Chicago Heights
entries.summary: <p>Two drivers were killed and three minors were hospitalized in a five-vehicle crash Friday afternoon in suburban Chicago Heights. </p><p>The crash happened around 4:30 p.m. at the intersection of Chicago Road and Joe Orr Road, according to Chicago Heights police.</p><p>Two drivers were pronounced dead at the scene, and the Chicago Heights Fire Department took three minors to area hospitals with injuries, police said. Their ages and conditions weren’t immediately available. </p><p>Anyone with information regarding this accident is encouraged to contact the Chicago Heights Police Department at 708-756-6400.</p>

entries.title: Guard Josh Giddey returns to watch Bulls embarrassed in Big Apple
entries.summary: <p>As far as Bulls guard Josh Giddey was concerned, it wasn’t a fluke.</p><p>When the Bulls opened the season 5-0, it wasn’t because they were playing bully against teams such as the Wizards and Nets. No, they had a season-opening victory against the Eastern Conference-leading Pistons and beat playoff-caliber teams such as the Magic, Hawks and Knicks.</p><p>There was something there in late October — months ago that feel like years, especially in the wake of an embarrassing 136-96 loss Friday to the Knicks.</p><p>‘‘I’ve said this before, but I really think we started off the season the right way,’’ Giddey said. ‘‘We were building momentum with the group we had, and then obviously at the deadline things changed.’’</p><p>Maybe. But things had changed before that, thanks to injuries, inconsistent defense and more mediocrity from a group that had toiled in mediocrity for too long. The front office had to make changes, which were long overdue.</p><p>With only five games left in the season, however, Giddey wasn’t done trying to search for something positive. As bad as the season has gone, there is still something worth salvaging, he said.</p><p>‘‘We blew up half our team, and we kind of went from building momentum with the guys we had to, like, a minicamp at midseason, trying to get guys acclimated to what we’re doing,’’ Giddey said. ‘‘So, yeah, it was challenging. It was challenging for everybody. It’s not like it was just me or one other guy. Everybody had to go through it. The front office makes the decisions they make, and it’s our job to play and go out there and win games. We haven’t done that nearly even close to a high-enough level.</p><p>‘‘But it’s about finishing the right way and doing the right things, staying with it. At the end of the day, it’s the NBA, and we don’t take that for granted. We need to finish this off the right way, regardless of playoffs or not.’’</p><p>The ‘‘right way’’ at this point would be the Bulls navigating the final stretch by using Giddey — and the other known pieces — in games in which there is an obvious talent disadvantage and allow him to rest his hamstring against fellow tankers such as the Wizards and Mavericks.</p><p>Giddey missed the Bulls’ game Wednesday against the Pacers but was back at it Friday against the Knicks. It wasn’t exactly an ideal matchup to come back for.</p><p>Knicks big man Mitchell Robinson scored the first basket of the game 45 seconds in, and who would have guessed that would have been enough to keep them in front until midway through the first quarter?</p><p>A free throw by Matas Buzelis was all the Bulls could muster until Collin Sexton made a three-pointer with 5:25 left in the first. By that point, the damage had been done, and Giddey and the Bulls were down 20-4.</p><p>By the end of the second quarter, the Knicks had the largest halftime lead in franchise history. They led by 37 points and got very little resistance. They had made 30 of 51 shots (.59%) from the field and had outrebounded the Bulls 31-18.</p><p>How bad was it for Giddey and his teammates? They had more turnovers than field goals midway through the second quarter and finished the half with 14 field goals to 11 turnovers. The Knicks, meanwhile, only turned the ball over twice.</p><p>By the end, Sexton led the Bulls with 19 points. Giddey, meanwhile, shot 3-for-12 from the field and committed four turnovers.</p><p>While there was no defense for that kind of showing, the Bulls are under a darker cloud than Giddey would admit. Coach Billy Donovan might walk away at the end of the season, and the front office is in limbo.</p><p>And while Giddey was trying to stay optimistic, the inevitable appears to be coming.</p>

entries.title: White Sox surprise Ozzie Guillen by retiring his No. 13
entries.summary: <p>There have been few things in baseball that have reduced <b>Ozzie Guillen</b> to tears. This was one of them.</p><p>The longtime <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> player, World Series-winning manager and beloved broadcaster was caught by surprise during the early innings of the CHSN telecast Friday when one of his former players on the 2005 title-winning team, <b>Scott Podsednik</b>, read from a statement announcing that the club was retiring Guillen’s No. 13.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Ozzie Guillen tears up while learning the Chicago White Sox will retire his number later this season <a href="https://t.co/bBU1FP5zkN">pic.twitter.com/bBU1FP5zkN</a></p>— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) <a href="https://twitter.com/awfulannouncing/status/2040147233929113955?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The number will be retired in pregame ceremonies Aug. 8, the Sox said.</p><p>‘‘That’s one of the biggest surprises I’ve ever had in baseball,’’ Guillen said of the honor, the thought of which gained momentum last year during the 20th-anniversary celebration of the 2005 team, when numerous former players said he deserved it.</p><p>‘‘I guess [the White Sox] did it the right way because they made me cry,’’ Guillen said. ‘‘I know how important this moment is for my family, myself. That shows you, shows myself that the White Sox cared what I did for them.’’</p><p>Guillen, who began his big-league career with the Sox in 1985, said he originally asked for No. 9 but was told he couldn’t have it because it had been worn by <b>Minnie Minoso</b> and had been retired two years earlier. Guillen then asked for No. 13, the number worn by his baseball hero, fellow Venezuelan shortstop <b>Davey Concepcion</b> of the Reds.</p><p>He said he hopes Concepcion, who will be 78 this summer, will be able to attend the retirement ceremony. He also is looking forward to 90-year-old chairman <b>Jerry Reinsdorf</b> being there, as well.</p><p>‘‘I just talked to Jerry a few minutes ago,’’ Guillen said. ‘‘He said, ‘I did want to see you cry once.’ ’’</p><p>Guillen has made a lasting impact on the Sox in multiple ways.</p><p>‘‘I’ve been lucky in Chicago, man,’’ he said. ‘‘A lot of people knew me as a player, a lot of people knew me as a manager and a lot of kids know me as that crazy guy on TV.’’</p><p>Guillen then delivered a classic ‘‘Ozzie-ism’’ when describing how much Reinsdorf means to him.</p><p>‘‘I never deny it, I love Jerry Reinsdorf more than my own dad,’’ Guillen told a media scrum gathered at the back of the press box during the game. ‘‘You know why? My dad, every time he calls me, he asks me for money. Jerry makes me money.’’</p><h3>Burke delivers</h3><p>Right-handers <b>Grant Taylor</b> and <b>Sean Burke</b> made a compelling case against panic Friday after the Sox’ pitching staff had allowed 52 runs in the first six games.</p><p>Taylor, serving as the opener, set down the Blue Jays in order in the first inning. And Burke, after yielding back-to-back doubles to start the second, didn’t allow another run in six strong innings. He struck out seven and walked none.</p><p>‘‘I think just in general, coming off a bad week of baseball, I really wanted to go out there in front of our home fans . . . and I just really wanted to entries.title: Cubs' offense 'not good enough' in loss to Guardians
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Something was off with the Cubs on Friday.</p><p>Aside from <b>Cade Horton</b>’s injury status being up in the air, the team looked discombobulated, particularly in the seventh.</p><p>Reliever <b>Hunter Harvey</b> needed 30 pitches to get through ⅔ of an inning, allowing three runs on two hits with a walk and no strikeouts. Right-hander <b>Jacob Webb</b> relieved Harvey and needed 12 pitches to get the final out.</p><p>Aside from the runs, the team unraveled in the seventh. There was the fielding error by center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> that allowed Guardians All-Star <b>Jose Ramirez</b> to advance to second after his line-drive single. Second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> also bobbled a routine ground ball before getting the out at first to end the inning.</p><p>Though Horton's injury loomed over the game, the Cubs still weren’t good enough in Friday’s 4-1 loss to the Guardians.</p><p>“Offensively, that just wasn't enough today,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “We didn't create traffic, really. We created one inning of good scoring [opportunities] and didn't cash in on it, but not enough offensively.”</p><p>The Cubs were 1-for-6 with runners in scoring position.</p><p>After <b>Miguel Amaya</b>’s RBI double in the third inning, the Cubs totaled just 2 hits the rest of the game. The offense failed to put much pressure on Guardians left-hander <b>Joey Cantillo</b>, who cruised throughout Friday’s game, controlling the Cubs’ lineup.</p><p>Cantillo was good at “playing the front and back game” with his velocity. He generated most of his whiffs (six of 10) with his changeup that flummoxed the Cubs’ lineup.</p><p>“His changeup is just kind of a floating changeup, but [it] just feels like it never gets there,” Counsell said. “So you either get it off the end or you get beat by a fastball.”</p><h3><b>ABS one-week review</b></h3><p>The implementation of the Automated Ball-Strike System was going to take some time for teams to adjust to. Though many focus on the number of calls that umpires get wrong, Counsell is looking at it from a different perspective.</p><p>“We've had some games already where it's like, ‘Man, that umpire was unbelievable,’” Counsell said. “And I wish that would actually get highlighted a little more in this new system. We should highlight how good some of the umpires are, which we don't, but we should.</p><p>“I mean, the first day of the Angels series, the umpire was brilliant; he was incredible. [He saw] 270 pitches [and] he missed, like, two of them."</p><p>Entering Friday, catcher <b>Carson Kelly</b> had challenged four calls behind the plate, winning three and losing one. He’s gained two strikes and eliminated a walk through six games.</p><p>But Counsell is holding off on judging ABS until after three weeks, which he feels is an appropriate amount of time to assess the system. He wants to see more information about it proliferate through more video and data.</p><h3><b>Suzuki rehab assignment</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Right fielder <b>Seiya Suzuki </b>began his rehab assignment at Double-A Knoxville on Friday. Suzuki is recovering from a PCL strain that he suffered playing for Team Japan in the World Baseball Classic.</p><p>The plan is for him to play five innings in right field, and Suzuki could return on entries.title: White Sox provide a happy day for Jerry Reinsdorf, fans in extra-inning home-opening win over Blue Jays
entries.summary: <p>A few months into his 10th decade, Jerry Reinsdorf had one of his better days as chairman of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a>. So did the fans of his team, which has spent far too much time on the dark side of the moon in recent years.</p><p>First, the 90-year-old Reinsdorf made Ozzie Guillen cry. Then the Sox, returning home after a dreadful 1-5 start in which they allowed a major-league-high 52 runs, gave him reason to smile.</p><p>The tears came on TV early Friday afternoon, when Guillen was told during the live broadcast on CHSN that Reinsdorf had given his blessing to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-ozzie-guillen-retire-number-13" target="_blank" >retire Guillen’s No. 13 Sox jersey</a>.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-ozzie-guillen-retire-number-13" >White Sox surprise Ozzie Guillen by retiring his No. 13</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-fans-optimistic-on-opening-day-despite-seasons-rocky-start-hope-never-dies" >White Sox fans optimistic at home opener despite season’s rocky start: ‘Hope never dies’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>‘‘I told him I was happy to make him cry,’’ Reinsdorf said of honoring Guillen, who played and managed on the South Side beginning in 1985 before becoming the cult figure he is today.</p><p>The smiles came in the aftermath of the home opener, Reinsdorf’s 46th as chairman of the team, with the Sox defeating the Blue Jays 5-4 after a head-spinning 10th inning that nearly made Japanese slugger Munetaka Murakami’s day end in embarrassment.</p><p>Murakami was pulled inches off first base by a wide throw from third baseman Miguel Vargas. The Sox challenged the call on what would have been an inning-ending play, but replays upheld the safe call by umpire Junior Valentine. Vargas was charged with a throwing error, and ghost runner Davis Schneider scored the go-ahead run.</p><p>The Sox then staged a face-saving — and game-winning — rally in their half of the 10th, scoring twice on a daring two-out bunt that traveled the length of a pool cue, followed by a walk-off delivered by a former Savannah Banana.</p><p>Outfielder Tristan Peters, whose continued employment as a ballplayer once depended in part on his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/02/white-sox-savannah-bananas-tristan-peters" >skill as a line dancer for the Bananas</a>, stroked his game-winning liner into right field against Jays closer Jeff Hoffman, then was chased into short center by a pack of delirious teammates.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="in" dir="ltr">TRISTAN. PETERS. <a href="https://t.co/GaBlnobkNe">pic.twitter.com/GaBlnobkNe</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2040175965477687458?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">April 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>‘‘I think they lifted me by the jersey,’’ Peters said, ‘‘and it ripped a few buttons off. But I don’t know how I ended up [shirtless].’’</p><p>Peters spent 17 games with an early incarnation of the Bananas before being drafted by the Brewers in the seventh round in 2021. The Sox purchased him from the Rays in December, he had a good spring in Arizona and, with Brooks Baldwin out with a sprained elbow, won a spot — at least temporarily — in the outfield.</p><p>Peters, one of 13 new players on the Sox’ roster, came into this season with a dozen big-league at-bats. A week into his first season with the Sox, he can claim a walk-off in the home opener.</p><p>‘‘I mean, this has got to be at the top,’’ he said. ‘‘This is just one of the coolest things. I mean, I’ve been playing every day so far since Opening Day, which has been great. I mean, just getting my at-bats, seeing pitching at the big-league level, it’s awesome. I’m just trying to be consistent.’’</p><p>The man who provided the bunt was the well-traveled Derek Hill, a former first-round draft choice by the Tigers a dozen years ago who is on his sixth big-league team in the last four seasons. In the midst of all his travels, Hill has made sure to pack his well-honed ability to bunt.</p><p>Clearly, a two-out bunt in extra innings with your team down by a run is not a high-percentage play. But the Jays had just lost their catcher, Alejandro Kirk, when he was struck in the thumb of his catching hand by a foul tip, and Ernie Clement, who had just been shifted to third, was playing back. All that registered with Hill and manager Will Venable, who decided to go for it.</p><p>Hill dropped his bunt down the third-base line, just a few feet from the plate. But backup catcher Tyler Heineman, who had been rushed into the game to replace Kirk, threw the ball into right field. Ghost runner Vargas scored the tying run before Hill dashed across the plate on Peters’ hit.</p><p>‘‘The opportunity presented itself, and thank God we knocked it out’’ — Hill paused before he caught himself — ‘‘not knocked it out but dropped it in the park. How far? Six feet, maybe.’’</p><p>Far enough to allow Reinsdorf to depart the ballpark a happy man, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/03/white-sox-fans-optimistic-on-opening-day-despite-seasons-rocky-start-hope-never-dies" >along with 33,171 who had come</a> in search of something to cheer about.</p><p>Reinsdorf has not done interviews in years, but he chatted briefly with an ink-stained acquaintance who said he last had spoken with him in a champagne-soaked clubhouse in 2005, when the Sox won the World Series,</p><p>‘‘A long time ago,’’ Reinsdorf said. ‘‘But it seems like yesterday. We need better pitching. The rest of the ballclub is OK, but we need pitching. And we need some wins.’’</p><p>And the South Side congregation said, ‘‘Amen.’’</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true"
